correctness.rationale: Open domination plus open independence forces each selected vertex to have one selected neighbor, and distinct matching components share neither row nor column. Two empty lines on the same side duplicate signatures; an empty row in the presence of a horizontal edge gives the singleton of that edge's endpoint twice (and dually for columns). This forces the three occupancy regimes. Conversely a mixed-board unselected signature has horizontal/vertical counts (3,0), (2,2), (1,1) or (0,3); the pure triple contains a unique matched pair and a singleton, and in mixed signatures the vertex types identify which pieces encode row and column. All are nonempty, injective and nonsingleton, whereas the selected signatures are distinct singletons. In a pure case the optional empty column (row) produces distinct pairs. The mixed allocation has m!n! ordered choices and symmetry factor 2^(h+v)h!v!; the pure allocation has n!/2^m or its transpose, including the choice of the optional empty line. The square-board specialization and exclusion of m=1 or n=1 are consistent.
residual_risks: Independent brute force checked all even subsets on 12 bounded boards, including exact counts 9 on (3,3) and 180 on (4,5); the all-board claim depends on the signature and allocation proof, not on enumeration.

value.rationale: As a mathematical result, the full classification of a natural all-vertex open-code notion on a canonical product is useful. The general selected-edge necessity does not prove sufficiency in graphs with triangles and four-cycles; here the signature profiles resolve that obstacle and give both the existence obstruction and the exact labeled family. This judges the substance of the theorem, not distinctness from the equivalent coverage recorded under originality.
residual_risks: No extrapolation to higher Cartesian powers or other location-domination notions.
